passage: Anjali, put the phone down a minute. You say Mr Bose's class is pointless because he picks on you. I said the same at fifteen about my chemistry teacher, Mrs Dias. Your Nani Elizabeth was no saint then. She asked me the hardest questions, and I was sure she wanted me to fail, so I stopped doing her homework and sat sulking on the back bench. Two terms of marks slipped away. Then I began writing things down: the date, what she asked, what she said. When I read the list, half of it looked less unfair than I'd thought. The other half still stung. So I asked to speak to her after school and told her plainly how it felt. She was surprised. She didn't turn into an angel, but she dropped the sharpest remarks. And I had to work to win my marks back, because the marks were mine, not hers.

qa.q: What did young Elizabeth write down in her list about Mrs Dias?
qa.a: The date, what she asked, and what she said.

qa.q: Why did Elizabeth stop doing Mrs Dias's homework?
qa.a: She felt targeted by the hardest questions and was sure Mrs Dias wanted her to fail, so resentment made her stop trying.

qa.q: What would you advise Anjali to do about Mr Bose's class?
qa.a: Note down specific examples, ask him for a private talk, and keep doing the work, since the marks are hers either way.

qa.q: How might Mrs Dias have seen the private talk?
qa.a: With surprise. That suggests she hadn't realised how her remarks landed, and afterwards she dropped the sharpest ones.

grounding: An elder recalls resenting a teacher, sulking, then gathering examples, talking privately and working on.

passage:
Sabina was sure Vikas sir had it in for her. He'd marked her down for handwriting when others wrote worse. He'd sent her out of class for whispering, though two boys had started it. By October she'd stopped doing his accounts homework altogether. What was the point?
Her mother found her at the dining table in their Kochi flat, scribbling angrily in a notebook.
"What's that?"
"Things Vikas sir does to me."
Her mother read the list. "Some of these look unfair. Some might just be bad days. Why not ask to see him alone and show him the clearest ones?"
"He'll just shout."
"Maybe. But your marks are yours, not his. Don't give them away because you're angry."
On Friday, Sabina asked Vikas sir if she could speak to him after class. Her voice shook. She showed him two marked papers side by side. He looked at them, frowned, and said, "You may be right about this one."

qa.q: Why did Vikas sir mark Sabina down?
What was Sabina feeling when she stopped doing the homework?
qa.a: She felt resentful and targeted, believing Vikas sir had it in for her, and saw no point in trying.

qa.q: Which steps did Sabina take that worked, and why?
qa.a: She gathered examples, chose the clearest ones and asked for a private talk, while her mother reminded her the marks are her own.

qa.q: How might Vikas sir see the moment Sabina shows him the papers?
qa.a: He seems surprised and willing to reconsider, admitting she may be right about one paper.

grounding: A teen who feels a teacher targets her and stops trying gathers examples, asks for a private talk and keeps working.

passage:
"Shalini ma'am, could I talk to you for five minutes? Privately?"
"Sachin. Yes, if it's quick. What's this about?"
"I feel like you pick on me in class. And I've stopped trying in chemistry because of it."
"That's quite a claim."
"I wrote down three times. On Monday you asked only me to stand when four of us were late. Last week you said my lab notes were 'the usual mess' in front of everyone. And when I got the titration right, you said 'finally' instead of 'good.'"
"Hm."
"I might be reading too much into some of it. But it made me feel like there's no point."
"I didn't realise the 'finally' sounded like that. And the late thing, you're right, I should have called all four."
"Thank you, ma'am."
"But Sachin, stopping work only hurts you. Your marks are yours."
"I know. I'll hand in the pending lab notes by Friday."
"Good. And my door's open if it happens again."

qa.q: How many students were late on Monday?
What was Sachin feeling before he asked to talk?
qa.a: He felt resentful and discouraged, as if there was no point trying in chemistry because the teacher picked on him.

qa.q: What made Sachin's talk with Shalini ma'am effective?
qa.a: He asked privately, gave specific examples, admitted he might be reading too much into some, and agreed to keep working.

qa.q: How does Shalini ma'am see Sachin's concerns?
qa.a: She seems surprised and reflective, admitting some of it was unfair while reminding him that stopping work only hurts him.

grounding: A teen who feels a teacher targets him gathers examples, asks for a private talk and decides to keep working.
